Leveraging the versatile but orthogonal reactivities of MNBN, a three-step cascade sequence, including nitrile cyclotrimerization, Knoevenagel condensation, and reductive cyclization, achieved the symmetrization, reticulation, and functionalization in one pot, thereby enabling the hierarchical construction of two series of COFs with stable o-nitrostyrene or indole linkages. The resulting COFs displayed high crystallinity, permanent porosity, and exceptional stability; solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (SSNMR) experiments combined with selective isotopic-labeling synthesis further confirmed the high selectivity and controllability of the hierarchical assembly. Notably, the indole-linked COFs, featuring conjugated and electron-rich frameworks, displayed emergent photoelectronic properties and served as efficient, reusable catalysts in both metal-free photocatalytic and metallaphotoredox reactions. By hierarchically exploiting the intrinsic reactivity of a simple, unsymmetric molecule, this work bridges classical organic synthesis and cross-scale covalent assembly, achieving the programmable construction of stable, diversified, and functional COFs.

item.title: A Dynamic Self-Reporting Metal–Organic Framework System for Catalysis and Real-Time Reaction Monitoring
item.description:
Abstract
Modern catalysis research has primarily focused on improving catalyst activity, selectivity, and stability through active-site engineering, microenvironment regulation, and mechanistic understanding. However, the sustainability and efficiency of catalytic processes also depend on the dynamic evolution of reaction systems, including substrate consumption, catalyst deactivation, and product accumulation. Despite their importance, these changes are typically assessed by off-line analysis rather than real-time monitoring, which hinders efficient process optimization and sustainable operation. Here, we develop a dynamic self-reporting (DSR) catalytic system based on Ag@UiO-66-(COOH)2/NDCA that simultaneously functions as a heterogeneous oxidation catalyst and an optical reporter for reaction progress. During oxidation, the emission intensity at 440 nm increases with product formation and exhibits a strong quantitative correlation with benzaldehyde yield, enabling reaction progress to be continuously tracked across a series of substituted benzyl alcohols. Mechanistic studies indicate that the luminescence response is governed by competitive absorption and substrate-dependent interactions. Density functional theory calculations further reveal that benzyl alcohol forms stronger dispersion-stabilized π···π interactions with the emissive NDCA2– linkers than benzaldehyde, resulting in more pronounced luminescence quenching. As benzyl alcohol is converted into the more weakly interacting product, this quenching is progressively relieved, producing a measurable increase in emission intensity that reports the reaction progress. This integration provides a platform for reaction monitoring, process optimization, and future automated manufacturing.

item.title: Luminescent Timeline from Confined Active Radicals Enables Infinite Cryptograph
item.description:
Abstract
The development of encryption materials is essential to meeting the increasing demand for information security. However, the present materials are susceptible to duplication due to a finite numbers of crypto states. Here, we report one chemical method to expand anticounterfeiting information from discrete, finite states to continuous, infinite states in the temporal domain by regulating the chemical reactions of luminescent radicals with the assistance of image-analysis technology. Infinite cryptographic materials were fabricated with continuous dynamic luminescence processes by integrating reversible radical reactions into confined radical luminescent systems. The inherent chemical kinetics of active radical emitters can be converted to time-dependent emission curves, serving as unclonable keys with nearly infinite crypto states in the temporal domain. Fluorescent AIE molecules were then introduced to expand the color gamut, further enriching the encoding capacity. These infinite cryptographic materials offer a robust anticounterfeiting platform, providing novel pathways for high-level information-protection applications.

item.title: Protecting Groups as Catalysts: Direct Synthesis of Primary Amines from Ammonia under Carbonyl Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Primary amines are indispensable building blocks in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and functional materials, yet their direct, modular synthesis from ammonia remains challenging. Here we report a carbonyl catalysis strategy that enables the direct synthesis of structurally complex primary amines from ammonia by integrating the conventional multistep sequence of protection, N–H functionalization, and deprotection into a single catalytic cycle. As a proof of concept, amino-trifluoromethylation of alkenes using ammonium salts and Togni reagent afforded a wide range of β-trifluoromethylated primary amines, including derivatives of complex natural products. 1,8-Diazafluorenone was uniquely competent as a carbonyl catalyst, highlighting the critical role of catalyst design in ammonia transformation. Mechanistic studies suggest that its distinctive electronic structure facilitates the formation of the N–H ketimine intermediate, a prerequisite for catalytic turnover. These findings establish carbonyl catalysis as a platform for the direct transformation of ammonia and demonstrate how protecting groups can function as catalysts.

item.title: Complementary Acetonitrile Reduction and Amine Adsorption on Mixed Cu–Ni Oxides for Electrocatalytic N-Ethylation
item.description:
Abstract
N-ethylamines are important motifs in pharmaceuticals and fine chemicals, but their selective synthesis from nitriles requires control over both nitrile reduction and amine availability at the catalyst-electrolyte interface. Herein, we investigate mixed Cu–Ni oxides for the aqueous electrocatalytic C–N coupling of acetonitrile (MeCN) with benzylamine (BA). The optimized Cu-NiO-0.5 catalyst affords N-ethylbenzylamine (EBA) in 75% yield with 87% selectivity and a mass-normalized formation rate of 12.5 mmol h–1 gcat–1 at −0.5 VRHE. Electrochemical testing indicates that the presence of CuO can promote the MeCN electrochemical reduction, generating abundant ethylimine for subsequent coupling. Meanwhile, the incorporation of Ni significantly enhances the adsorption of BA, accelerating the C–N coupling between the ethylimine and BA. In situ experimental measurements further confirm the sequential reduction-condensation-reduction pathway. Moreover, this strategy has also been proven to enable efficient C–N coupling between MeCN and various amine derivatives, giving the corresponding N-ethylated products in 58.3–84.6% yield and greater than 74% selectivity. This work offers an environmentally friendly strategy for the electrocatalytic synthesis of N-ethylamines.

item.title: A Stable Phosphinidene Radical Anion as a Multielectron Reducing Agent
item.description:
Abstract
The diagonal relationship between carbon and phosphorus has long inspired comparisons between the chemistries of carbenes and phosphinidenes. However, while carbene chemistry has flourished over the past three decades, isolable phosphinidenes remain exceptionally rare, and their one-electron reduction products, phosphinidene radical anions, are unknown. Here, we report the synthesis and isolation of a crystalline phosphinidene radical anion through one-electron reduction of a ring-strained phosphanorcaradiene, a phosphinidene equivalent. Structural, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal a monocoordinate phosphorus center where the unpaired electron is predominantly localized, in line with a highly reduced phosphorus center. The radical anion exhibits multielectron redox reactivity, including radical addition to an arylalkyne, sulfur atom transfer from isothiocyanate, elemental chalcogen activation, and stepwise oxidation to high-valent P(V) compounds through an overall five-electron process, integrating formal paramagnetic P(0)/P(II)/P(IV) radicals and diamagnetic P(I)/P(III)/P(V) derivatives.

item.title: Cooperative Enantiomorphic-Site and Chain-End Chirality in Isoselective β-Lactone Polymerization
item.description:
Abstract
Polymer properties are profoundly impacted by tacticity, necessitating an understanding of the origins of stereocontrol to make high-performance materials. Recently, we reported that controlled incorporation of stereoerrors into trans-poly(3-hydroxy-2-methylbutyrate) (trans-PHMB) through the isoselective polymerization of rac-trans-3,4-dimethylpropiolactone (trans-DMPL) using racemic “sandwich” (BDI)Zn alkoxide complexes (where BDI = β-diketiminate) enables tuning of mechanical properties to match those of low-density polyethylene. However, the mechanism of stereocontrol of these catalysts was not explored. Herein, we report a thorough experimental and computational investigation uncovering a distinct manifestation of cooperative enantiomorphic-site and chain-end control, which we describe as site-mediated asymmetric chain-end control, where catalyst (Δ and Λ) and chain-end chiralities (R,R or S,S) work synergistically to influence the reaction’s stereoselectivity and rate. Experimental and computational data converge remarkably well, revealing that a Δ-catalyst with an (R,R)-chain end (Δ-RR) is isoselective 90% of the time. In contrast, a Δ-catalyst with an (S,S)-chain end (Δ-SS) is unselective. Detailed Density Functional Theory (DFT) investigations suggest molecular-level rationale for this mechanism of stereocontrol, demonstrating that chain positioning, monomer distortion, and ligand interactions work in conjunction to foster isoselectivity. Finally, DFT and kinetic modeling reveal that when polymerizing rac-trans-DMPL, the populations of Δ-RR and Δ-SS are equal and the high overall isoselectivity (mm% = 71–73%; where mm% is the percent of triads with a meso configuration across both ester linkages) of the catalyst is attributed to Δ-RR being faster than Δ-SS.

item.title: Perfluoroalkyl Anion Strategy to Construct Anion–π + Type NIR-II Phototheranostic Agents for Enhanced Tumor Immunotherapy via Necroptosis/Ferroptosis
item.description:
Abstract
Anion-π+ photosensitizers (PSs) possess exceptional reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and precise organelle targeting that could disrupt intracellular metabolic homeostasis and induce nonapoptotic cell death, offering unique advantages in overcoming immunosuppression. However, previous reports mainly focused on modifying the π+ core but often overlooked the crucial role of anions. Herein, we present a facile perfluoroalkyl anion strategy to modulate the fluorescence intensity and ROS generation capacity of anion-π+ PSs. Perfluorobutanesulfonate (PFB) anions with a single-sided perfluoroalkyl chain and bis(perfluorobutylsulfonyl)amide (BPFB) anions bearing double-sided perfluoroalkyl chains were employed to readily replace the hexafluoroantimonate (HFA) counterions in A/HFA and TPQ/HFA, yielding A/PFB, TPQ/PFB, A/BPFB, and TPQ/BPFB. Compared to the incorporated PFB anions, the BPFB anions more effectively restrict intramolecular motion through anion-π+ and van der Waals interactions, thereby significantly enhancing the fluorescence intensity of the phototheranostic agents─by 50.8-fold and 4.2-fold in A/BPFB nanoparticles (NPs) and TPQ/BPFB NPs compared to their HFA analogues, respectively. Concurrently, TPQ/BPFB NPs with second near-infrared emission demonstrated superior ROS generation, excellent mitochondrial targeting, and remarkable resistance to photobleaching. Strikingly, TPQ/BPFB NPs can activate both necroptosis and ferroptosis under irradiation, triggering a robust systemic immune response. Additionally, the lipophilicity granted by BPFB enables TPQ/BPFB NPs to infiltrate deeper into tumors, guaranteeing a more extensive photodynamic therapy with a 95% tumor suppression rate. Crucially, the immune memory triggered by TPQ/BPFB NPs effectively decreases the occurrence of lung metastases. Altogether, the perfluoroalkyl anion strategy proposed in this study offers new insights for developing potent anion-π+ PSs.

item.title: MetallopeptiGELs: Injectable Short-Peptide Supramolecular Hydrogels Self-Assembled by Pd Nanosheets for Bioorthogonal Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Controlling the delivery of chemotherapy to the tumor site is a long-standing goal of the medical field, as it could not only enhance the anticancer activity of the treatment but also reduce damage to the rest of the body. The emergence of bioorthogonal catalysis as a strategy capable of mediating continuous drug production in a nonenzymatic fashion has created the opportunity to develop so-called “bioorthogonal therapies,” which aim to generate the anticancer agents inside the tumors. Herein, we describe a novel class of supramolecular materials comprising ultrathin palladium nanosheets and fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl-diphenylalanine that self-assemble in water to form injectable, self-healing, biocompatible catalytic gels that convert inactive prodyes and prodrugs into active small molecules. The relatively weak physicochemical cross-links generated by the hybrid metal-peptide fibers facilitate the flow of the gel under mild shear stress (shear-thinning), thereby enabling precise intratumoral injections in vivo and localized prodrug activation. The strategy was validated in an aggressive pancreatic cancer xenograft model in mice, setting out a new direction for the field of bioorthogonal therapies.

item.title: Carbon Insertion into Electron-Deficient (Aza)indoles via a Radical-Polar Crossover Strategy
item.description:
Abstract
Despite a surge of progress in both strategic approaches and reagent design, carbon insertion into indoles remains limited to electron-rich substrates, notwithstanding the prevalence of electron-poor (aza)indoles in medicinal chemistry. We report herein a radical-polar crossover strategy that overcomes this limitation through a photocatalytic, iodomethyl-radical-mediated cyclopropanation/autoxidation approach. The method enables access to a range of highly substituted, electron-poor quinolines, naphthyridines, and triazanaphthalenes, many of which are challenging to prepare by traditional syntheses. We demonstrate the modification of medicinally relevant (aza)indoles, and preliminary mechanistic observations support autoxidation via an anionic cyclopropane ring opening pathway.

item.title: Scalable Fluorinated Copper-Based Covalent Organic Frameworks for Coupled Ultratrace Perfluoroalkyl Substances Monitoring and Efficient Remediation
item.description:
Abstract
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent water contaminants that require both effective removal and reliable monitoring. However, these functions are typically performed separately, preventing real-time evaluation of treatment performance. Here we establish a cooperative host–guest-coupling principle, in which a single host–guest binding event simultaneously drives contaminant capture and modulates the Cu-centered redox process, thereby generating concentration-dependent electrochemical signals within a porous framework. Guided by this principle, we reported a scalable fluorinated copper-based covalent organic framework (F–Cu–COF) synthesized through an open-air one-pot strategy that enables gram-scale production while retaining high crystallinity and chemical stability. Fluorinated pore domains and redox-active Cu centers create a cooperative host–guest environment that promotes PFAS binding and enrichment with electrochemical signal generation. Consequently, F–Cu–COF achieves a detection limit of 5.2 pg L–1, an uptake capacity of 3824 mg g–1, and efficient flow-through removal. This work establishes host–guest coupling as a common molecular basis for linking electrochemical signal generation with contaminant capture in scalable porous materials, providing a general design strategy for multifunctional water-treatment platforms capable of integrated treatment verification.

item.title: Interhalogen of Iodine Chloride Accelerates Charge Transfer for Efficient Li 2 O 2 Oxidation in Lithium–Oxygen Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Li–O2 batteries suffer from sluggish Li2O2 oxidation kinetics at electrode/electrolyte interfaces, leading to large charge polarization and low energy efficiency. Soluble redox mediators (RMs) provide a solution-mediated pathway for Li2O2 decomposition and reduce the charge overpotential. However, the chemical oxidation of Li2O2 by oxidized RMs remains kinetically sluggish, resulting in persistent charge polarization. Herein, iodine monochloride (ICl), an interhalogen compound, is electrochemically generated in situ during the charge process to promote the oxidation of Li2O2. The large electronegativity difference between I and Cl promotes intramolecular charge transfer from I to Cl, creating an electrophilic iodine center (Iδ+) that increases the I–Cl bond polarity and strengthens the interaction with Li2O2. This lowers the decomposition barrier of Li2O2 from 2.39 to 0.77 eV, thereby facilitating its chemical oxidation. The Li–O2 battery delivers a low discharge/charge polarization of 0.52 V, effectively mitigating parasitic reactions at high voltages and enabling an extended cycling lifespan exceeding 800 h. This work provides a valuable design principle for developing redox mediators for efficient Li2O2 oxidation.

item.title: Support Protection Mechanism Enables Efficient and Stable Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers
item.description:
Abstract
Designing oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalysts that simultaneously achieve high activity and long-term stability remains a critical challenge for the development of alkaline anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs). Here, we uncover a unique support protection mechanism in which lattice-confined ruthenium (Ru) single atoms offer robust protection for the spinel Co3O4 support, realizing outstanding stability in AEMWEs. Theoretical calculations and structural characterizations reveal that lattice confinement promotes the formation of robust Ru–O–Co bridges by simultaneously shortening the Co–O and Ru–O bond lengths, thereby suppressing Co dissolution and optimizing the electronic structure for efficient catalysis. Furthermore, in situ electrochemical analysis demonstrates that the lattice confinement of Ru atoms accelerates OER kinetics through facilitated proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) steps and partially activated lattice oxygen. As a result, the RuLCA-Co3O4 dominated by the adsorbate evolution mechanism (AEM) exhibits a lower overpotential of 260 mV at 10 mA cm–2, which is lower than that of RuSCA-Co3O4 dominated by the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) pathway. Meanwhile, the lattice-confined RuLCA-Co3O4 exhibits nearly 9-fold lower Co dissolution compared to surface-coordinated RuSCA-Co3O4 after an accelerated durability test (ADT). Moreover, RuLCA-Co3O4 maintains an outstanding stability for over 1000 h in an AEMWE system with a low degradation rate of 88.1 μV h–1, outperforming RuSCA-Co3O4. This work establishes lattice confinement as an effective strategy to decouple activity-stability trade-offs in alkaline OER and provides a viable design principle for durable AEMWE anodes.

item.title: Decoupling Dissolution from Water Oxidation at Single-Faceted High-Entropy Perovskite Electrodes
item.description:
Abstract
High-entropy oxides (HEOs) are promising anode materials for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) due to their wide compositional space and electronic flexibility. However, their electrochemical dissolution and OER remain concurrent, preventing decoupled analysis of dissolution kinetics and stability. Here, we present a combined atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) strategy to decouple lattice dissolution from water oxidation under well-defined reaction conditions. Structurally analogous, atomically flat, single-faceted (001) ABO3 perovskite electrodes, La1–xSrx(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Co0.2Ni0.2)O3 with x = 0 and 0.3, serve as model systems to probe dissolution and OER kinetics in acid. Pipet-probed localized cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry reveal that the measured current contains contributions from both OER and lattice dissolution, the latter producing nanoscale dissolution pits beneath the SECCM droplet. By correlating pit-growth kinetics with total OER charge as a function of pulse duration (τ), overpotential (η), and pH, we quantitatively separate dissolution from OER. The proportional scaling between dissolution charge and total charge indicates that OER and dissolution proceed within a common kinetic regime, sharing a common intermediate. A rate-law-based analysis yields the standard dissolution rate constant (kd0 cm/s), transfer coefficient (α), and proton reaction order (b) for the dissolution of the 001 facet of both HEO-P. Our results unravel how aliovalent A-site substitution (30% Sr2+) alters dissolution kinetics, charge partitioning between dissolution and OER, and thickness-dependent stability, thereby enabling quantitative disentangling of the intrinsic activity and stability of HEO electrodes.

item.title: A Pseudo-Icosahedral RhH 2 Au 10 Superatom: Two Hydrogen Atoms Acting as Gold-Atom Equivalents and Modifiers
item.description:
Abstract
A hydrogen atom is known to act as a gold-atom-equivalent dopant in gold nanoclusters (AuNCs) by contributing to the valence electron count. To gain insights into the interaction of multiple H atoms with AuNCs, we herein synthesized a di-H-atom-doped NC, [RhH2Au10(dppp)5]3+ (RhH2Au10; dppp = 1,3-bis(diphenylphosphino)propane), by exposing [RhAu10(dppp)5]3+ (RhAu10) to H2 gas; RhAu10 was generated in situ via hydride (H–) abstraction from [RhHAu10(dppp)5]2+. Comprehensive characterization of RhH2Au10 by X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, and theoretical calculations revealed that the two H atoms occupy the two “missing” Au sites in the arachno-type RhAu10 core via dissociative adsorption of H2, forming a pseudo-icosahedral RhH2Au10 core. This core structure contrasts sharply with the previously reported di-H-atom-doped silver- or copper-based superatoms, in which the H atoms form an MH2 (M = Os, Ru, Rh) unit completely encapsulated within an icosahedral Ag12 or Cu12 shell. The RhH2Au10 core possesses an 8-electron closed-shell electronic configuration of (1S)2(1P)6, which is isoelectronic to the icosahedral RhAu12 superatom, thereby demonstrating the Au-atom equivalence of H atoms. Nevertheless, the two H atoms in the RhH2Au10 superatomic core act as structural modifiers compared to the RhAu12 superatom: (1) the degeneracy of the 1P orbitals is lifted by lowering the geometric symmetry, and (2) the HOMO–LUMO energy gap is expanded due to the reduced electronic confinement volume. This study demonstrates that multiple H atoms in a gold-based superatomic core not only behave as Au-atom equivalents but also serve as key components for modulating their fundamental properties.

item.title: Enhancing Propanol Production from CO 2 Reduction with a Terbium-Doped Copper Nitride Electrocatalyst
item.description:
Abstract
Propanol is one of the most complex products obtained from CO2 electroreduction (CO2R). Being an interesting precursor for synthetic fuels and a feedstock for the chemical industry, its electrochemical production has recently raised increasing interest. However, low selectivity for propanol has been achieved so far. Here, via exploring a variety of original lanthanide-doped copper nitride materials, we identified and characterized terbium-doped copper nitride as the most selective catalyst for propanol formation. It allowed CO2R to yield propanol with a Faradaic efficiency of 27% at a high current density of 300 mA cm–2 within a neutral (KHCO3 electrolyte) flow cell, surpassing the performance of previous CO2R catalysts. The high density of undercoordinated nitride-derived Cu sites, combined with the increased oxophilicity of the surface, likely promoted the selectivity toward alcohols. Thorough DFT calculations showed that Tb doping increased the affinity for oxygenate-associated C2* intermediates and lowered the free-energy barrier for reactions coupling the latter with CO* toward propanol.

item.title: Layer-Distortion Engineering of Acridinium-Based Covalent Organic Frameworks Enables Efficient Photoredox Transformations of Alcohols
item.description:
Abstract
Planar two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (COFs) often suffer from severe interlayer π–π stacking, which promotes excitonic recombination, restricts access to active sites, and compromises photocatalytic efficiency. Here we report a layer-distortion engineering strategy to construct wavy acridinium-based COFs, Mes-Acr-TAPB and Mes-Acr-TAPP, by introducing structural distortion into otherwise planar layered frameworks. The resulting wavy framework efficiently suppresses interlayer π–π stacking, enlarges interlayer spacing, modulates molecular packing, pore environment, and improves accessibility to photoactive acridinium sites. Compared with the planar analog Dur-Acr-TAPB, Mes-Acr-TAPB exhibits enhanced exciton dissociation along with substrate absorption, more efficient charge separation, and superior photocatalytic activity. As a heterogeneous photoredox catalyst, Mes-Acr-TAPB enables diverse alcohol transformations under mild conditions, including β-scission radical functionalization, ring contraction/expansion, and skeletal transposition. Mes-Acr-TAPB shows broad functional-group tolerance and supports late-stage structural modification of complex natural products, highlighting its synthetic utility. This work establishes layer-distortion as an effective design principle for mitigating interlayer stacking in 2D COFs and advancing high-performance COF photocatalysts for sustainable organic synthesis.

item.title: Kinetic Control of Polymorphism in Li 10.5 Si 1.5 P 1.5 S 12 –Based Solid Electrolytes
item.description:
Abstract
Li10GeP2S12 (LGPS)-type solid electrolytes (SEs) are among the most promising materials for next-generation solid-state batteries (SSBs) due to their high lithium-ion conductivity. However, challenges related to phase stability and polymorphism, especially in Ge-free, Si-based systems, limit their practical implementation. Here, the crystallization and phase transition behavior of materials with a nominal composition of Li10.5–xSi1.5P1.5S12–xIx (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4) are systematically investigated. Operando high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction, total scattering with pair distribution function analysis, and differential scanning calorimetry measurements reveal the formation of a metastable orthorhombic (o) phase, followed by transformation into the thermodynamically stable tetragonal (t) phase at elevated temperatures. Our findings indicate that lithium iodide (LiI) as an additive regulates the crystallization of the o-phase and thereby governs the transition kinetics. This enables the o-to-t phase transition to occur at much reduced temperatures and faster rates. Neutron powder diffraction further uncovers minor modifications to the Si/P ratio and lithium sublattice, as well as the fact that iodine is not incorporated into the t-phase; instead, a secondary Li4PS4I-type phase forms. Collectively, this work highlights the critical role of microstructural engineering on crystallization and polymorphism in LGPS-type SEs and also demonstrates the applicability of these dual-phase materials by enabling high-performance lithium–sulfur SSBs.

item.title: Efficient Chemical Synthesis and Enzymatic Replication of 3′-Deoxyapionucleic Acid (ApioNA): An RNA-Selective XNA with Conformational Flexibility
item.description:
Abstract
Xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs) have emerged as versatile platforms due to their sugar scaffolds that enable precise chemical tuning, leading to distinct classes ranging from fully compatible systems to orthogonal systems. However, sugar-modified XNAs capable of discriminating between RNA and DNA have remained elusive. In this work, we establish 3′-deoxyapionucleic acid (ApioNA) as a structurally flexible XNA with inherent RNA-selective hybridization properties. We achieved efficient production of ApioNA oligonucleotides through an efficient asymmetric synthesis of their building blocks and systematically characterized their properties. Thermal melting analyses demonstrate that ApioNA forms moderately stable duplexes with RNA while exhibiting weak pairing with DNA and negligible self-association. Quantum mechanical calculations reveal that the apiofuranose ring populates two low-energy puckering states, and the addition of an extra methylene group enhances backbone flexibility, thereby favoring A-form geometry for RNA pairing while requiring a higher-energy state to accommodate B-form DNA. Despite its weak affinity for DNA, ApioNA supports a complete enzymatic replication cycle using commercial Therminator and Bst 3.0 polymerases with approximately 98% fidelity and is processed by native E. coli machinery in vivo. This work fills the RNA-selective niche in the XNA functional landscape and establishes sugar puckering dynamics and backbone flexibility as key design principles for programming nucleic acid pairing specificity.

item.title: Boosting Ionomer Oxygen Transport via Pore Confinement in Carbon Supports for Low-Pt Fuel Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Low-Pt proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are promising for hydrogen energy implementation, yet oxygen transport through ionomer-covered catalyst surfaces becomes increasingly limiting due to the resistance associated with dense ionomer films. Herein, we demonstrate a pore-confinement strategy to manipulate the spatial locality of Pt nanoparticles within porous carbon supports, enabling simultaneous regulation of ionomer distribution and molecular organization. Pt nanoparticles were selectively positioned on the external surfaces (Ptext/PC) or within the internal nanopores (Ptint/PC) of otherwise comparable supports, while maintaining similar Pt loading, particle size, and pore characteristics. Under H2-air condition, Ptint/PC delivered a peak power density ∼1.3 times higher than that of Ptext/PC, but a similar current density in the high-voltage region. Electrochemical analyses reveal that the performance enhancement originates from improved oxygen transport rather than catalytic activity. Wide-angle X-ray scattering and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the Pt nanoparticles confined within mesopores disrupt the dense packing of ionomer backbones, thereby boosting oxygen permeability at the catalyst–ionomer interface. By establishing a direct relationship between Pt locality, ionomer distribution, backbone organization, and oxygen transport, this work identifies catalyst locality as an effective parameter for engineering interfacial mass transport and provides a new design principle for low-Pt PEMFCs.

item.title: Electrochemical Synthesis of Slaked Lime Utilizing a Diaphragm Flow Cell
item.description:
Abstract
Slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) is one of the most widely utilized chemicals, with applications in diverse industries including construction, mining, water treatment, and chemical manufacturing. Currently, Ca(OH)2 is synthesized by coal-fired calcination of CaCO3 to make CaO, followed by exothermic hydration. Converting CaCO3 into Ca(OH)2 using electrochemically generated acid and base has attracted great interest because it could be powered by renewable electricity and would generate the CO2 byproduct in a pure form. Previous electrochemical Ca(OH)2 syntheses have incorporated the processing of calcium salts within the electrochemical cell to avoid acid–base recombination losses, but these cells have poor stability and high energy demand. Herein, we show that production of high-salinity acid and base solutions using a diaphragm flow cell (DFC) coupled with ex situ processing of CaCO3 substantially improves the efficiency of electrochemical Ca(OH)2 production. Using a closed loop with a simple KCl salt solution, we demonstrate the synthesis of >99% pure Ca(OH)2 for 0.088 to 0.10 kWh per mole at productive current densities of 158 to 334 mA cm–2.

item.title: Synthetic W/Cu Mimics of the Mo/Cu Active Site in Aerobic CODH: Nonclassical Isocyanide Coordination and the Role of the Bridging Sulfide
item.description:
Abstract
Aerobic carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH) uses an unsupported Mo–S–Cu heterobimetallic active site to catalyze CO oxidation, but the mechanistic role of the bridging sulfide remains to be fully resolved. We report a series of W/Cu complexes designed to test whether steric shielding from a bidentate tBuxantphos ligand can suppress unwanted Cu···Sdithiolate and Cu···O═M interactions that plagued the reactivity of a previously reported NHC-ligated model system. Addition of [Cu(tBuxantphos)]+ to [(bdt)WVI(O)(OSiiPr3)(X)]− (bdt = 1,2-benzenedithiolate; X = O, S, Se) unexpectedly favors Cu coordination at the W═O rather than the W═X unit, giving X═W–O–Cu cores as the thermodynamically preferred isomers, opposite to the connectivity predicted by hard–soft acid–base theory and found in CODH itself. The resulting complexes bind isocyanides at CuI with nonclassical (blue-shifted) C≡N stretching frequencies. In contrast, no reactivity is observed toward CO gas, consistent with DFT predictions that CO coordination is endergonic. However, the calculations reveal that the CO adduct of the hypothetical O═W–S–Cu–CO isomer is more stabilized than its S═W–O–Cu–CO counterpart, an effect traced by molecular orbital analysis to delocalization of electron density from the redox-active dithiolate through the bridging sulfide into the Cu–CO π-backbonding manifold. These results provide an electronic rather than purely structural rationale for why the CODH active site retains a bridging sulfide despite an apparent thermodynamic preference for a bridging oxo in the synthetic analogues investigated here.

item.title: Intricate Proteoform Heterogeneity in the Tailpiece of IgA within and across Its Circulatory and Secretory Configurations
item.description:
Abstract
Human immunoglobulin A (IgA) naturally occurs in multiple molecular forms─monomers, dimers, and even higher-order polymers─that are differentially distributed across serum, breast milk, and mucosal surfaces. The C-terminal tailpiece of IgA is essential to its polymerization mediated by the joining chain (J-chain) and thus also an important determinant of its extensive structural heterogeneity, yet its features remain somewhat poorly defined. Here, we used HILIC-LC-MS/MS-based glycopeptide analysis to characterize the N-glycan structures, disulfide linkages, and C-terminal amino acid sequence variants within the IgA tailpiece across the different molecular configurations of endogenous IgA. We find extensive correlation between these post-translational modifications; i.e., variations in tailpiece Asn459 N-glycosylation, redox status and disulfide connectivity of Cys471, and the presence or absence of C-terminal Tyr472 are intrinsically interconnected. When Cys471 was disulfide-bound to the J-chain, Asn459 glycans showed broader structural heterogeneity and retained more high-mannose structures, whereas free Cys471 tailpieces mainly carried mature, sialylated complex-type glycans. Serum IgA and milk SIgA displayed distinct tailpiece signatures, including differences in N-glycan maturation and processing of the ultimate C-terminal Tyr472 residue. Together, these findings define biofluid-specific molecular forms of IgA and highlight the remarkable structural diversity of the human IgA tailpiece. Overall, our results advance the understanding of the IgA structure and could offer a much-needed molecular basis to assist future bioengineering of IgA-based therapeutics.

item.title: A Microporous Zr-Tetraphosphonate MOF with Permanent Porosity, Robustness, and Thermochemical Heat Storage Capability
item.description:
Abstract
Combining high-valent metal cations with phosphonate linkers represents a promising strategy to address the limited stability of MOFs, yet permanently porous phosphonate MOFs (P-MOFs) remain rare due to the strong coordination propensity of phosphonate groups. Herein, we report IEF-10, a new microporous zirconium tetraphosphonate framework constructed from ZrO5F octahedral secondary building units and a pyrene tetraphosphonate linker. The material combines three features that are seldom achieved simultaneously in P-MOFs: permanent accessible microporosity (equivalent BET surface area ∼430 m2·g–1), accessible phosphonic acid functionalities (-PO3H), and exceptional thermal (up to 450 °C), mechanical (>3 tons), and chemical stability (pH 1–12, organic solvents). The structure exhibits reversible water adsorption with moderate uptake and experimentally determined capacities of heat storage of ∼400–500 J·g–1, reflecting a favorable balance between host–guest interactions and regeneration requirements. As a proof of concept, IEF-10 was evaluated for thermochemical heat storage under dynamic moist-gas flow conditions. Calorimetric measurements revealed fast heat-release kinetics (3–4 h), and excellent cyclability in terms of heat release (at least 10 cycles, total test duration of 5 weeks). The hydrophobic surface character is an advantage for long-term storage uses as the adsorbent can remain in a dry state between the charging and discharging stages even at low relative humidity levels in the reactor. These results demonstrate how the combination of permanent porosity, accessible phosphonic acid groups, and exceptional framework robustness can enable functional adsorption-driven energy storage while providing new opportunities for the development of porous zirconium P-MOFs.

item.title: Fluorine-Mediated Molten-Salt Crystallization Regulates Phase Evolution and Structural Stability in Sodium Layered Oxides
item.description:
Abstract
Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered oxides with high Na concentrations are promising cathodes for sodium-ion batteries, but their practical use is limited by phase instability during Na-excess synthesis and structural degradation during cycling and storage. Although large single-crystal-like architectures could improve stability, controlled phase-selective crystallization in these cathode systems remains challenging. Here, we show that fluorine-assisted molten-salt synthesis enables controlled formation of large-particle Fe–Mn–Ti P2 cathodes with enhanced phase selectivity and structural coherence. Compared with Na-excess processing alone, NaF-assisted flux growth expands the P2 phase stability window and promotes large particles with uniform morphologies while preserving local layered ordering. Multiscale characterization further reveals more-reversible structural evolution and more homogeneous Mn redox behavior in the NaF-assisted material, together with a gradient-like fluorine distribution involving surface-enriched NaF-like species and lower level interior fluorine environments. These coupled structural, morphological, and chemical features collectively mitigate crack formation and deliver good cycling stability. In summary, NaF-assisted molten-salt synthesis shows promise in addressing key limitations of Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered cathodes.

item.title: G-Quadruplex-Interacting Photooxidative Platinum(IV) Prodrug for Inhibiting Oncogene Transcription and Amplifying Antitumor Immunity
item.description:
Abstract
Conventional platinum (Pt)-based chemotherapeutics elicit cancer cell death primarily through DNA binding, but this approach is inherently limited by poor site specificity and a lack of spatiotemporal control, which compromises therapeutic precision and safety. To overcome these limitations, we report DNATplatin, an in situ activatable and photooxidative Pt(IV) prodrug designed to combine precise recognition of DNA secondary structures with targeted genetic intervention through DNA photooxidation. By incorporating a bis-N-methylpyridinium moiety to selectively recognize DNA, DNATplatin shows a 10-fold increase in the levels in genomic DNA relative to oxaliplatin and a 2.5-fold emission turn-on selectivity for G-quadruplexes (G4s) over typical duplex DNA. Following precise nuclear localization, photoactivated DNATplatin acts as a potent photooxidant that oxidizes G4, dismantles G4 scaffolds, and abrogates circular dichroism signatures. These orchestrated lesions generate localized oxidative stress and selectively silence major G4-driven oncogenes, thereby effectively circumventing traditional Pt resistance by bypassing canonical adduct-dependent pathways. In a murine triple-negative breast tumor model, DNATplatin produces profound tumor suppression and elicits a robust systemic immune response, characterized by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell activation and depletion of Foxp3+ regulatory T cells. Collectively, this work establishes a controllable “target-and-destroy” strategy and underscores the potential of Pt(IV) photooxidants for topology-selective genetic intervention.

item.title: Sugar-Based 1-Dimensional Metal–Organic Chalcogenolates with Hydration-Tunable Chiroptical Emission
item.description:
Abstract
Chiral topology in semiconductors introduces a structural degree of freedom for tuning the chiroptical, excitonic, and spintronic behavior. In metal–organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) semiconductors, how ligand stereochemistry and supramolecular organization influence chiral topology, and thus optical and excitonic responses, remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate intrinsic circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) in sugar-based 1-dimensional MOChas, with structures solved via small-molecule serial femtosecond crystallography. These materials exhibit blue and green CPLs, arising from the chiral inorganic core. Despite the close chemical similarity between the glucose- and galactose-derived ligands, we observed dramatic differences in their inorganic structure. Silver glucosethiolate shows reversible hydration-driven photoluminescence switching with a hydration-linked emission energy. Labile water molecules in the glucose-based system correlate with a blueshift in excitonic emission. Our results suggest a new direction in the search for chirophotonic hybrid semiconductors, exploiting intrinsically chiral topologies and excitonic optical frequencies, which are sensitively modulated by ligand identity and supramolecular interactions.

item.title: Core–Shell Structures Govern Through-Space Interactions in Triblock Copolymers toward Deep-Red Clusteroluminescence
item.description:
Abstract
Green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its derivatives have transformed biological imaging, yet fluorophores that simultaneously combine biocompatibility, structural programmability, and intrinsic long-wavelength luminescence remain scarce. Here, we develop a controllable one-pot polymerization strategy to construct nonconjugated triblock copolymers that can self-assemble into core–shell clusters. By modulating the hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance of copolymer chains, the core-to-shell ratio, chain packing, and electronic through-space interactions within the clusters can be precisely regulated, enabling tunable clusteroluminescence (CL) that extends to the deep-red and near-infrared emission region. Ultrafast spectroscopy further uncovers the excited-state dynamics of these core–shell clusters and reveals how the coupled evolution of electronic states and structures governs CL generation. Moreover, the core–shell clusters enable in vivo angiography under two-photon excitation, highlighting their potential as biocompatible nanofluorophores. These findings establish core–shell engineering as a general design principle for efficient clusteroluminogens, deepen the mechanistic understanding of CL, and pave the way for next-generation nanofluorescence technologies.

item.title: Modifier-Driven Proton Conductivity in Hybrid Glasses above 200 °C
item.description:
Abstract
Compositional tuning is a cornerstone of inorganic glass science, yet analogous strategies remain underdeveloped for emerging metal–organic hybrid glasses. We introduce phosphate modification of zinc imidazolate glass as a route to hybrid glasses with tunable network connectivity and proton-conductive functionality. Melt-quenching of ZIF-zni with benzimidazolium dihydrogen phosphate (BP) affords a series of cm-scale, transparent bulk glasses across a wide compositional range. Systematic characterization reveals that modification proceeds through ligand exchange at zinc centers, increasing the average coordination number from 4 to above 5 and progressively depolymerizing the imidazolate network. Despite macroscopic homogeneity, X-ray total scattering identifies a quasi-periodic ordering at ∼11 Å, and 1H NMR spin relaxation establishes nanoscale phase segregation between ZIF-derived and BP-rich domains of 2–70 nm. This heterogeneity underpins proton transport under anhydrous conditions; conductivities of 10–5–10–3 S cm–1 at 240 °C follow Vogel–Tammann–Fulcher dynamics, confirming that segmental motion couples to ion mobility. Infiltrating the glass into a porous PTFE scaffold yields a composite membrane that achieves 8.4 × 10–5 S cm–1 at 170 °C under humidification and sustains steam electrolysis with near-unity Faradaic efficiency. These results establish network-modified hybrid glasses as a scalable and designable platform for intermediate-temperature solid electrolytes.

item.title: Crossover from Asymmetric to Symmetric Electrowetting Linked to Double-Layer Restructuring
item.description:
Abstract
Voltage-controlled wetting at solid–liquid interfaces is central to the performance of a range of electrochemical and microfluidic technologies, yet the molecular basis of polarity-dependent electrowetting remains unresolved. Classical electrocapillarity predicts a symmetric dependence of contact angle on applied potential, but experiments and simulations frequently exhibit pronounced asymmetry. Here, combining electrowetting measurements with atomistic simulations, we show that asymmetric wetting at aqueous carbon interfaces arises from the structure of the electrical double layer. By investigating aqueous KF and LiCl electrolytes at graphitic interfaces across lower concentration and water-in-salt regimes, we identify a crossover from strongly asymmetric electrowetting at lower concentration to a symmetric response at high concentration for KF, while LiCl retains a pronounced asymmetry. This transition is accompanied by corresponding changes in the solid–liquid interfacial tension, demonstrating that polarity-dependent wetting can arise from voltage-dependent molecular restructuring of the interfacial liquid, which modifies the interfacial thermodynamics, without invoking faradaic processes. We introduce interfacial connectivity, defined by the network of intermolecular interactions within the first adsorption layer, as a molecular descriptor linking double-layer structure to macroscopic wetting behavior. These results demonstrate that electrolyte-controlled electrowetting can recover the symmetric electrocapillary limit under appropriate conditions and establish a unified framework connecting double-layer structure, interfacial free energy, and voltage-dependent wetting.

item.title: Energy Deposition Timescales Controls Chemistry in Pulsed Methane Plasmas
item.description:
Abstract
Nonoxidative methane conversion offers a promising route for the coproduction of hydrogen and value-added hydrocarbons without CO2 emissions. Among emerging approaches, pulsed plasmas can provide potential advantages by enabling high energy deposition, rapid quenching, and generation of active nonthermal species. This work systematically investigates how pulsed energy deposition from nanosecond-to-millisecond time scales (10 to 50 mJ/pulse) influences methane plasma characteristics (electron density and gas temperature), reaction mechanisms, conversion, and energy efficiency. Nanosecond discharges produced the highest overall C2 selectivity (>70%), with up to 20% for C2H4; in this regime, methane dissociation proceeded through both electron-impact and thermal dissociation, whereas longer pulses were predominantly thermal. Pulsed plasma conversion was similar to thermal arcs (∼377 kJ/mol CH4) and specific energy requirements to produce C2H2 and H2 were 15 kWh/kg and 40 kWh/kg, respectively, in 100 μs long discharges. The product distribution was largely determined by thermal processes involving dehydrogenation reactions (Kassel’s reaction scheme). High gas temperatures preferentially favored C2H2 formation over C2H4, and C2H4 selectivity decreased with increasing pulse width. Overall, these results demonstrate that pulse width and energy can be used to tailor hydrocarbon selectivity and can help design pulsed plasma systems for efficient production of value-added hydrocarbons and hydrogen.

item.title: Sky-Blue Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence from a Zirconium(IV) Complex
item.description:
Abstract
Earth-abundant early transition-metal complexes with luminescent ligand-to-metal charge-transfer (LMCT) excited states remain an attractive yet underexplored alternative to widely used precious-metal emitters. A fundamental understanding of the molecular design principles governing the photophysical properties of LMCT emitters is critical to further developing cost-effective and sustainable photochemical applications using this compound class. Here, we report the synthesis of a novel bis(4,5-ditolylamido-9,9-dimethylxanthene)zirconium complex, Zr(TolXDA)2, that shows efficient photoluminescence due to thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) at room temperature. Steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic studies at room temperature reveal highly efficient and long-lived emission in the sky-blue and green wavelength range for solid samples (λPL = 480 nm, ΦPL = 0.60, τPL = 4–14 μs) and THF solutions (λPL = 548 nm, ΦPL = 0.30, τPL = 8 μs) of Zr(TolXDA)2, respectively. Despite the relatively large singlet–triplet energy gap (ΔEST ≥ 0.26 eV), TADF emission in Zr(TolXDA)2 is unambiguously confirmed by temperature-dependent emission studies. This is likely facilitated by the high LMCT character of the S1 and T1 states, a consequence of strategic ligand design, which allows for rapid forward and reverse intersystem crossing. This hypothesis is supported by femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, which confirms facile forward and reverse intersystem crossing in Zr(TolXDA)2 (τISC = 15 ± 5 ps, τrISC = 0.48 ± 0.39 μs), and TD-DFT calculations, which establish significant negative charge transfer to zirconium in the lowest energy excited states.

item.title: Physically Grounded Descriptors for Machine-Learning-Guided Diluent Design in Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Localized high-concentration electrolytes require diluents that avoid direct Li+ coordination and preserve Li+-anion aggregates while remaining miscible with the primary solvent. Rational discovery has remained difficult because these competing requirements arise from chemically distinct interactions that have lacked computable molecular design coordinates. Fluorination has therefore been widely used to suppress electron donation, but the environmental persistence and synthetic burden of fluorinated molecules motivate alternative strategies for controlling diluent functionality. Here, we resolve the key interaction requirements of diluents using two complementary descriptors: BF3 affinity for specific electron-pair donation and the molecular polarity index (MPI) for distributed nonspecific electrostatic interactions. These descriptors reproduce established donor-number and Kamlet–Taft π* trends and, more importantly, distinguish noncoordinating yet miscible diluents from solvating and immiscible solvents. Coupling this interaction-based framework with uncertainty-aware machine learning enabled screening of 1.32 million nonfluorinated molecules and identified 368 candidates while recovering false negatives and excluding false positives near the decision boundaries. Newly selected aromatic hydrocarbons, including 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene and 2-ethyltoluene, sustained stable cycling in Li-metal full cells for more than 200 cycles, whereas a descriptor-excluded analogue underwent rapid capacity decay. These results establish specific coordination and distributed electrostatics as predictive design coordinates for diluent discovery.

item.title: Microenvironment-Directed Galvanostatic Base Generation for Near-Neutral Hydrolysis of a Nerve-Agent Simulant
item.description:
Abstract
Organophosphate hydrolysis under near-neutral conditions is intrinsically slow and generally requires strongly basic media or tailored catalysts. Here, we demonstrate that the electrolyte microenvironment can promote hydrolysis of dimethyl 4-nitrophenyl phosphate (DMNP) through an electrochemically generated base. Chemical controls show that DMNP hydrolysis depends on the combined effects of bulk pH, phosphate speciation, electrolyte concentration, and substrate accessibility. Under galvanostatic operation, cathodic water reduction generates OH– in situ, coupling hydrogen evolution to specific-base SN2(P) hydrolysis of DMNP. Time-resolved 31P NMR shows reciprocal DMNP consumption and dimethyl phosphate formation, while complementary UV–vis spectroscopy is consistent with formation of p-nitrophenolate. Although K2HPO4 and NaClO4 provide similar DMNP conversion at the same current, phosphate lowers the required overpotential and substantially improves energy-normalized conversion efficiency. Translation to a zero-gap membrane-electrode assembly enables stable full-cell operation and quantitative DMNP consumption within 1 h in a larger-volume, flow-compatible configuration. These findings establish galvanostatic in situ base generation as a controllable and modular strategy for organophosphate treatment in near-neutral aqueous media.

item.title: Thiol-Mediated Hydrazide Installation from Diazo in the Biosynthesis of Spinamycin
item.description:
Abstract
Natural products featuring nitrogen–nitrogen (N–N) bonds often possess potent bioactivities, and their architectures frequently reveal novel enzymatic mechanisms. Current understanding for acylhydrazide installation is limited to a “hydrazine-first” strategy, wherein an activated acyl donor is nucleophilically attacked by a preassembled hydrazine intermediate. Spinamycin, an antifungal hydrazide-containing aryl polyene from Streptomyces albospinus, challenges this convention. Its biosynthetic machinery utilizes SpiA7, an ATP-dependent, nitrite-utilizing N-nitrosylase, to synthesize a highly transient diazo intermediate rather than a hydrazine core. How this unstable diazo compound is converted into a stable hydrazide has remained a long-standing biosynthetic mystery. Herein, we report the in vitro reconstitution of the activity of SpiA7 in conversion of the amine substrate into its mature succinylhydrazide form. Mechanistic characterization revealed that the electrophilic diazo intermediate is initially captured by thiol reagents to generate a covalent azo-sulfide intermediate (R–N═N–S–R′). This species likely undergoes a noncanonical four-electron reduction driven cooperatively by disulfide bond formation and the oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoglutarate (αKG), which serves as the succinyl donor. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis identifies Cys453 of SpiA7 as a likely active-site thiol donor orchestrating this transformation. Collectively, our findings unveil an unprecedented chemical strategy for hydrazide assembly that completely bypasses a free hydrazine intermediate, expanding nature’s known catalytic repertoire for building complex N–N linkages.

item.title: Bridging Ionic Field Strength Disparity in O3-Type Layered Oxides for High-Voltage Sodium-Ion Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
O3-type layered oxides represent an attractive class of sodium-ion battery cathodes, combining high theoretical specific capacity and high pristine Na content. However, their deeply desodiated frameworks at high voltages (≥4.0 V) are prone to redox-coupled distortion of TMO6 octahedra within the transition metal (TM) slabs, leading to severe structural degradation. Here, we originally define an ionic field strength disparity coefficient (η), which enables quantitative evaluation of the local chemical-field heterogeneity. The η is derived from the ratio between the standard deviation and the average value of ionic field strength (Φ) of all TM ions, defined as Φ= Z/r2, where Z and r correspond to the ionic charge and ionic radius, respectively. Introducing compensatory cations with an intermediate Φ value between two cations featuring largely disparate Φ values effectively reconciles local chemical-field discrepancy and lowers the η parameter upon charge–discharge processes. Moreover, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, strain mapping analyses, and first-principles calculations reveal that the low-η sample demonstrates the reduced lattice strain and enhanced structural reversibility. Consistently, electrochemical evaluation shows that it retains more than 80% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 10C, markedly outperforming the unmodified counterpart with only 22% retention. This work establishes the η as a quantitative descriptor for inactive dopant selection and provides a general strategy for developing highly stable layered oxide cathodes.

item.title: Molecule-Driven Unusual Incommensurate Modulation in a 2D Hybrid Perovskite Ferroelectric
item.description:
Abstract
Incommensurate modulation has been extensively investigated in inorganic oxides, representing an emerging frontier in aperiodic materials that enables the discovery of novel quantum phenomena and the manipulation of physical properties, whereas it remains largely unexplored in hybrid perovskites (HPs). Here, we present the driving of successive dynamic rotation of the interlayer dipoles in a two-dimensional HP ferroelectric (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 (DFBZ is 2,5-difluorobenzylammonium, FA is formamidinium), which enables an unusual incommensurate modulated structure between the paraelectric and ferroelectric phases. Specifically, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 exhibits an incommensurate modulated state over a broad temperature range of 313–370 K, and transforms to commensurate modulation at 400–474 K. The incommensurate superstructure at 330 K is ∼6 times larger than its periodic prototype, and its structure can be solved using a (3 + 1)D superspace group with a modulation wavevector of q = (1, 0, 0.1578). The inorganic layers feature a pronounced undulation, while the interlayer organic cations are trapped in distinct rotational states. To the best of our knowledge, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 is the first HP ferroelectric that exhibits such a long-range ordered incommensurate modulation. Moreover, its large spontaneous polarization (9.4 μC cm–2) and the near-room temperature ferroelectric-to-incommensurate phase transition result in a giant pyroelectric coefficient of 7.41 μC cm–2 K–1. This unusual incommensurate modulation in HP ferroelectrics offers new insights into the understanding of aperiodic materials and ferroelectric mechanisms.

item.title: A Route to Enhanced Energy Barriers and Reduced Magnetic Relaxation in Axial Bis(stannolediide) Lanthanidocenates
item.description:
Abstract
We report the synthesis and magnetic properties of one-dimensional lanthanidocenate coordination polymers, [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy; LSn = [1,4-bis(tert-butyl-dimethylsilyl)-2,3-bis-phenyl-stannolediide]). These were obtained by abstracting the solvent molecules from the potassium atoms of the corresponding monomers [Ln(η5-LSn)2K(thf)4]. The flexible coordination of the stannole dianion enables polymerization via potassium-mediated Sn–K–arene interactions, yielding linear chain structures while preserving a highly axial coordination environment around the Ln3+ center. Magnetic studies reveal that both [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy) compounds behave as single-molecule magnets in zero field, with significantly enhanced performance compared to their monomeric analogues. In particular, [Dy(η5-LSn)2K]n exhibits an increased effective energy barrier of Ueff = 1812 K, representing an improvement of ∼20%, alongside suppressed quantum tunneling of magnetization and slower relaxation dynamics. Detailed analysis of the relaxation mechanisms indicates that polymerization reduces spin–phonon coupling, as evidenced by a marked suppression of the Raman relaxation process, despite softer lattice vibrational modes. Ab initio calculations confirm the retention of highly axial electronic structures. These results demonstrate that assembling axial lanthanidocenate units into one-dimensional frameworks is an effective strategy to enhance magnetic anisotropy and control relaxation pathways, providing a route to mitigate relaxation in high-performance lanthanide-based single-molecule magnets.

item.title: Deoxygenative Metal Carbenation: A Strategy for Stereocontrolled Olefin Metathesis via an Oxo-Ruthenium Precursor
item.description:
Abstract
Dithiolene metathesis catalysts have enabled breakthroughs in materials and medicinal contexts in which control of cis/trans alkene stereochemistry translates into control over function. Their extreme air-sensitivity, however, impedes widespread uptake. Building on the discovery that air-exposure selectively decomposes the leading catalyst Ru(S–S)(H2IPr)(═CHAr) (Ru-1a; S–S = 1,2-S2C6H2-3,6-Cl2, Ar = C6H4-2-OiPr) into four-coordinate oxo complex Ru-2 Ru(O)(S–S)(H2IPr), we demonstrate that the latter offers convenient access to Ru-1a and related catalysts via reaction with phosphorus ylides (Ph3P═CHR; R = Ar, Ph, H). This “deoxygenative metal carbenation” (DMC) strategy opens new opportunities in olefin metathesis. Beyond regeneration of Ru-1a after decomposition, it enables direct, tunable access to more active on-cycle species (potentially including tagged benzylidenes) from a robust, shelf-stable precursor. In situ generation of these well-defined active species confers metathesis activity and stereocontrol comparable to or better than pristine, meticulously handled Ru-1a, and far superior to samples of Ru-1a even briefly exposed to air in solution. In eliminating the need for production, shipping, and storage of air-sensitive Ru-1a, this advance is anticipated to expand the uptake of olefin metathesis for production of stereodefined alkenes.

item.title: Directional Charge Transport via Interlayer Electronic Coupling Enhances Photocatalysis in Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description:
Abstract
The design of efficient photocatalysts requires control over both exciton dissociation and the subsequent transport of charge carriers. Donor–acceptor two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are widely used to promote charge separation, but the role of directional charge transport in these layered materials is still not well understood. Here, we combine photophysical characterization and time-dependent density functional theory calculations to study three TAPD-based COFs for photocatalytic H2O2 production via oxygen reduction. All materials show efficient in-plane donor–acceptor charge transfer with similar exciton dissociation behavior. At the same time, clear differences appear in their charge transport properties. The calculations indicate that electrons move preferentially along the stacking direction, while holes remain more delocalized within the COF plane. This anisotropic transport is most pronounced in the COFs where stronger interlayer coupling favors the formation of interlayer charge-transfer states, as observed in transient absorption measurements. These states allow electrons and holes to separate over adjacent layers, which reduces recombination losses and corroborates the observed differences in photocatalytic activity. Our results indicate that directional interlayer charge transport, rather than local donor–acceptor charge separation alone, is an important factor in determining photocatalytic performance in COFs.

item.title: Physics-Informed Site-Specific Molecular Interaction Learning Framework for Liquid–Liquid Phase Diagram Reconstruction and Extraction Process Design
item.description:
Abstract
Liquid–liquid phase behavior is governed by the collective balance of intermolecular interactions and is central to predicting component partitioning and designing extraction-based separation processes. Existing thermodynamic and data-driven approaches can predict phase-equilibrium properties, but provide limited resolution of the molecular-interaction-to-phase-topology relationship underlying coupled binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Here, PSMI is proposed as a physics-informed site-specific molecular interaction learning framework that reconstructs ternary liquid–liquid phase diagrams directly from molecular structures. PSMI learns chemically meaningful intermolecular interaction sites through molecular representation learning and integrates chemical-potential consistency regularization to guide thermodynamically reliable phase reconstruction. The framework predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions along continuous phase paths and enables reconstruction of binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Across benchmark tests, PSMI accurately predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions and recovers phase-diagram topology, including both binodal shapes and tie-line directions. Interpretability analysis shows that PSMI identifies transferable molecular drivers underlying liquid–liquid phase separation, including chemically meaningful interaction patterns. Industrial case studies, together with a locally deployable web application, further demonstrate the practical utility and accessibility of PSMI for solvent screening and extraction process design. By resolving site-specific intermolecular interactions together with their macroscopic phase-partitioning consequences, PSMI provides a molecular-level perspective on how local chemical environments contribute to liquid–liquid phase behavior. This connection between localized molecular interactions and continuous phase-diagram topology provides a framework for understanding and designing complex liquid–liquid separation systems.

item.title: Cryo-EM Structure of a Monomeric Safracin B Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Enabled by an MbtH-like Protein and Covalent Probe Trapping
item.description:
Abstract
Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) assemble structurally complex natural products but remain challenging targets for high-resolution structural analysis because of their conformational heterogeneity and dynamic catalytic cycles. SacC/SfmC is an unusual single-module NRPS that diverges from canonical peptide-forming assembly lines and instead catalyzes two sequential Pictet–Spengler reactions between a tyrosine-derived unit and a peptidyl aldehyde generated through thioester reduction. This cascade forms two C–C bonds, stereoselectively installs multiple stereogenic centers, and constructs the pentacyclic scaffold of bis-tetrahydroisoquinoline antitumor alkaloids including safracin B and the clinically important ecteinascidins. Here, we establish a state-resolved cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) strategy for structural interrogation of the monomeric noncanonical NRPS SacC and report its thioesterification-state structure at 2.76 Å resolution. Stabilization of this transient catalytic state was achieved by combining the cognate MbtH-like partner protein with a tailored covalent adenosine vinylsulfonamide probe that mimics the aminoacyl-adenylate intermediate and traps the phosphopantetheine-tethered species within the adenylation domain. The structure directly visualizes a carrier protein-tethered intermediate and reveals the spatial organization of the Pictet–Spengler, adenylation, peptidyl carrier protein, and reduction domains, providing the first structural view of a Pictet–Spengler cyclization domain embedded within an NRPS assembly line. In parallel, nonreducible ester probes corresponding to downstream PCP-bound intermediates were developed to enable structural interrogation of additional catalytic states along the SacC reaction trajectory. These results demonstrate that rational chemical probe design enables state-resolved cryo-EM analysis of highly dynamic, single-module NRPSs and establishes a general strategy for capturing catalytic trajectories and enabling the engineering of noncanonical NRPS reactivity.

item.title: Secondary-Sphere Control of Electronic Structure and Ligand Basicity in Mo-Nitrogenase: A QM/MM Analysis Guided by Se K-Edge HERFD XAS
item.description:
Abstract
Molybdenum nitrogenase catalyzes biological nitrogen fixation using a complex metallocofactor (FeMoco) containing three μ2-“belt”sulfides that exhibit distinct reactivity during catalysis. In particular, protonation at the S2B site imparts lability that facilitates substrate binding and may enable this sulfide to act as a proton donor. Although FeMoco is inactive outside its protein environment, how secondary-sphere residues tune its geometric and electronic structure to enable function remains unclear. We have previously shown that site-selective Se substitution of the μ2-sulfides provides a direct probe of the ligand environment using Se K-edge high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected X-ray absorption spectroscopy (HERFD XAS). Despite the cofactor’s approximate C3 symmetry, Se-substituted sites display pronounced differences in Se HERFD XAS pre-edge intensities. Utilizing QM/MM calculations, we show that hydrogen-bonding (H-bonding) residues polarize the S3A and S5A sulfides, reducing metal–ligand covalency and attenuating pre-edge intensity, whereas hydrophobic residues surrounding S2B localize electron density and enhance its pre-edge intensity. These results demonstrate how hydrophobicity and H-bonding within the secondary coordination sphere modulate FeMoco electronic structure. More broadly, they show how the protein environment tunes ligand basicity to favor selective S2B protonation and provide design principles for controlling enzymatic function.

item.title: Selective Methylation of Phenol with CO 2 /H 2 to o -Cresol and 2,6-Xylenol
item.description:
Abstract
Employing CO2/H2 as a sustainable methylating agent offers a transformative strategy for advancing conventional methylation processes, yet achieving controllable C–C coupling with high efficiency remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a novel tandem process that integrates CO2 hydrogenation with phenol methylation over a Zr-doped In2O3 solid-solution catalyst. The optimized In7Zr3Ox catalyst exhibits >95% selectivity toward ortho-methylation with tunable product distribution, ranging from 92% o-cresol at 16% conversion to 86% 2,6-xylenol at 97% conversion, while maintaining stable operation for 140 h. Mechanistic studies identify surface formaldehyde species (CH2O*) generated from CO2 hydrogenation as the active methylating intermediates that kinetically couple CO2 reduction to phenol methylation. This pathway exhibits a markedly lower apparent activation energy of 58.8 kJ mol–1 than the conventional methanol-mediated route of 116.3 kJ mol–1. Continuous consumption of CH2O* also shifts the CO2 hydrogenation equilibrium, imparting a thermodynamic driving effect absent in CO2 hydrogenation alone. These findings demonstrate the potential of CO2-based methylation for selective C–C bond formation and expand opportunities for CO2 valorization.

item.title: A New Paradigm for Computational Chemistry
item.description:
Abstract
Computational chemistry has become an indispensable tool for generating data and insights, pervading all branches of experimental chemistry. Its most central concept is the potential energy hypersurface, which is key to all chemistry and materials science, as it assigns an energy to a molecular structure, the necessary ingredient for reaction mechanism elucidation and reaction rate calculation. Density functional theory (DFT) has been the most important method in practice for obtaining such energies, which is reflected in the use of high-performance computing hardware. In the last two decades, a new class of surrogate potential energy functions has evolved with remarkable properties: quantum accuracy combined with force-field speed. Until very recently, their application was hampered by the fact that they needed to be trained on truly large system-specific data sets, generated before a computational chemistry study could be started (in sharp contrast to DFT, which, as a first-principles method, works out of the box but at a far higher price of computational cost). Very recently, this roadblock has been overcome by so-called foundation machine learning interatomic potentials, which are poised to completely change the way we do computational chemistry, likely prompting us to abandon DFT as the prime method of choice for this purpose in less than a decade.
